clue.text: More carefree bloke all but leader

indicators.note: everything except the front runner stays, so the opening letter is dropped

parts.note: a blighter is an informal British word for a chap or fellow

explanation.surface: Someone asks which chap is the more relaxed one, minus the one in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove B from BLIGHTER. 'Blighter' is dated British slang for a man, often a mildly annoying one.
explanation.definitionFit: Lighter in mood means less weighed down by worry, so more easygoing and cheerful.

clue.text: Most flamboyant ruffian hugging some Parisian

indicators.note: to hug is to wrap arms around, so one piece wraps around another

parts.note: a lout is a rough, uncouth man
des is French for 'some'

explanation.surface: A showy thug embraces a French person in the street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parisian' is the signal to translate 'some' into French rather than use an English word.
explanation.definitionFit: Loud clothes or manners are garish and showy, so the loudest person is the most flamboyant.

clue.text: Look good with simple changes

parts.note: G is the standard abbreviation for good

indicators.note: things that undergo changes are altered, so these letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Advice that a few easy tweaks will make you look good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look good' reads as a phrase about appearance, but 'Look' is the definition as a noun and 'good' is just G.
explanation.definitionFit: A glimpse is a quick, brief look at something, so the noun senses match.

clue.text: Spike Milligan's conclusion supporting Norse god

indicators.note: in a down clue a supporting piece holds up another, so it goes underneath

parts.note: Thor is the Norse god of thunder

indicators.note: a conclusion is an ending, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the surname

explanation.surface: The end of the comedian Spike Milligan's act propping up a Norse deity.
explanation.walkthrough: Spike Milligan was a British comedian, so 'Spike' looks like part of his name; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A thorn is a sharp pointed growth on a plant stem, a natural spike.

clue.text: Name rider developing balance

indicators.note: something developing is changing form, so these letters take a new shape

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A horse rider is building up their sense of balance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balance' reads as the rider's poise, but here it is the accounting sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The balance of a sum is what is left over after deductions, the part still owing.

clue.text: Expression of defiance from drunkard in this place

parts.note: a sot is a habitual drunk
here means at this spot

explanation.surface: A defiant shout from a drunk who is standing right here.
explanation.walkthrough: The enumeration 2,5 tempts a split after the second letter, but the wordplay breaks after the third.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a childish retort said after getting your own way, a mark of defiance.

clue.text: Milky drink Arab leader picked up

indicators.note: something picked up is heard, as on a radio set, so the word goes by its sound

parts.note: a sheikh is an Arab chief

explanation.surface: A milkshake ordered for an Arab ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arab leader' looks like it asks for a first letter A; it is a whole title, a sheikh.
explanation.definitionFit: A shake, short for milkshake, is a cold drink of milk whipped with flavouring.

clue.text: Ship rehearses leaving current harbour

indicators.note: whatever is leaving goes away, so that letter drops out

parts.note: to train is to practise or drill
I is the physics symbol for electric current
a port is a harbour

explanation.surface: A ship practises manoeuvres as it leaves harbour on the tide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' suggests the sea's flow but is I, removed from TRAINS. 'Ship' is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: To ship goods is to send or carry them from one place to another, the verb sense.

clue.text: Radical former lover Mike found in plane

parts.note: an ex is a former partner

indicators.note: something found in a place is inside it, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: the plane is a kind of tree
Mike is M in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A former partner, Mike, turns out to be a radical, discovered on a flight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plane' suggests an aircraft but is the plane tree, with M placed inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Radical and extreme both describe views far from the moderate mainstream.

clue.text: Old tree duly reduced by 50 per cent

parts.note: the elder is a tree

indicators.note: cutting something by half leaves only one of its two halves, here the back end

parts.note: the second half of the word

explanation.surface: An aged tree has been duly cut down by half.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the back half of DULY survives, giving LY.
explanation.definitionFit: Elderly is a polite adjective for people who are advanced in years.

clue.text: Identical thing potential Oxford student fills in?

definitions.text: thing potential Oxford student fills in?
definitions.meaning: second meaning, playful: the paperwork an applicant to a university completes

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a whimsical second meaning: split UNI FORM, the application a would-be undergraduate fills in.
explanation.definitionFit: Uniform as an adjective means unvarying, with every part matching exactly.

clue.text: Scotch tape dad adjusted

indicators.note: to scotch a plan is to wreck it, so these letters are broken up and rebuilt

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Father fiddled with the sticky tape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scotch tape' reads as the brand of sticky tape, hiding that 'Scotch' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something adapted has been altered to suit new conditions, just as a thing adjusted has.

clue.text: Sexy, naked and broody, dear?

indicators.note: stripped of its covering, a word loses its outer layer and keeps its middle

parts.note: the inner two letters of the word
broody here means moody and thoughtful

explanation.surface: Someone describes their darling as sexy, nude and moody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dear' looks like a term of endearment to the lover, but it means costly.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage dear means high in price, so costly goods are expensive.

clue.text: Box holding legionary's second weapon

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: to spar is to box in practice

indicators.note: the second position in a word picks out just that one letter

parts.note: the second letter of the word

explanation.surface: A chest containing a Roman soldier's backup weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Box' looks like a container noun but is the verb, to spar.
explanation.definitionFit: A spear is a long-shafted weapon with a pointed tip for thrusting or throwing.

clue.text: Flower pot's bottom split

indicators.note: the bottom of a word is its last letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word
a rent is a tear or split

explanation.surface: A flowerpot has cracked at the base.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' means something that flows, a river: the Trent runs through the English Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: In crosswords a flower is often a river, and the Trent is one of England's major rivers.

clue.text: Celebration on hospital department after male's medical care

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece on another sits above it
coming after something means following it in order

parts.note: a treat is a special celebration or outing
M is the abbreviation for male
ENT is the ear, nose and throat department

explanation.surface: A party on a hospital ward follows a man's medical care.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after 'male' stands for 'is', a linking verb in the wordplay rather than a possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: Treatment is the medical attention given to a patient to cure an illness or injury.

clue.text: Find dance music jolly

parts.note: disco is a style of dance music
in British slang 'jolly good' means very good

explanation.surface: Someone finds a dance track cheerful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Find' reads as a verb but is the noun, as in a lucky find; 'jolly' is the British intensifier for very.
explanation.definitionFit: A find is something valuable newly come upon, which is exactly a discovery.

clue.text: Occasionally so meek, oddly, on X

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece on another sits above it

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: taken oddly, a word yields only its odd-numbered letters

parts.note: the odd letters of the word, its first and third letters
X is the multiplication sign, read 'times'

explanation.surface: A mild person who now and then posts on the platform X.
explanation.walkthrough: X looks like the social network but is the times sign in arithmetic.
explanation.definitionFit: Occasionally and sometimes both mean now and then, at irregular intervals.

clue.text: You might hit this snag, almost, with racehorse

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is lost

parts.note: the word minus its last letter
Red Rum was a famous racehorse that won the Grand National three times

explanation.surface: Riding a racehorse, you might nearly hit a snag.
explanation.walkthrough: Red Rum is the legendary British steeplechaser; 'hit' in the definition means strike with a stick.
explanation.definitionFit: A drummer strikes this small drum with sticks, so it is a thing one might hit.

clue.text: Wife enthralled by yellowish bird

indicators.note: one enthralled by another is held captive, so it sits inside

parts.note: sallow describes an unhealthy yellowish complexion
W is the abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: A wife captivated by a pale yellow bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yellowish' seems to describe the bird but supplies SALLOW, which holds W.
explanation.definitionFit: The swallow is a small migratory songbird with a forked tail.

clue.text: Gold ridge somewhere in Central Europe

parts.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
a stria is a narrow ridge or groove

explanation.surface: A seam of gold along a mountain ridge in central Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: STRIA is a technical word, the singular of striae, meaning a thin raised line.
explanation.definitionFit: Austria is a landlocked country in the middle of the European continent.

clue.text: Swiss archer's orders

definitions.meaning: first meaning: belonging to William Tell, the Swiss folk hero who shot an apple off his son's head

explanation.walkthrough: The possessive 'archer's' reads as 'archer is' too, which is why TELLS with no apostrophe fits both.
explanation.definitionFit: To tell someone to do something is to instruct them, so tells means orders as a verb.

clue.text: Large boat nearly capsized by rear of the iceberg?

indicators.note: nearly means falling just short, so the final letter goes

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for large

indicators.note: a capsized vessel is upside down, so in a down clue the letters run the other way

parts.note: a cutter is a small ship, minus its last letter

indicators.note: the rear of a word is its last letter

parts.note: final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A big ship almost overturned by the back end of an iceberg, Titanic-style.
explanation.walkthrough: The iceberg that sinks ships is really a salad; the question mark flags that it is an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Iceberg is a crisp, pale variety of lettuce, so the definition is by example.

clue.text: Guys are dancing around Romeo? Not a thing you normally get in theatre

definitions.text: Not a thing you normally get in theatre

indicators.note: going around something means enclosing it
dancers move about, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
the contracted form 're, as in they're
Romeo is R in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: Men dancing around Romeo on stage, not the usual sight at a play.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Guys are' as GUYS'RE. The definition is a playful misdirection: an operating theatre is exactly where surgery happens, but a playhouse is not.
explanation.definitionFit: Surgery is what happens in an operating theatre, yet it is hardly what a playgoer expects.

clue.text: Benefit from dog scratching bishop

indicators.note: to scratch a name is to strike it out, so that letter is removed

parts.note: the basset is a short-legged hound
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A clergyman gains from having a dog scratch him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scratching' looks like a dog's habit but means crossing out, as a horse is scratched from a race.
explanation.definitionFit: An asset is a useful or valuable quality, a benefit to whoever has it.

clue.text: Tom may go in this vehicle that moves earth and rubbish

parts.note: a Cat is a Caterpillar tractor or bulldozer
litter is discarded rubbish

explanation.surface: A man called Tom rides in an earthmover full of junk.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom looks like a man's name but is a male cat, and 'go' means relieve himself.
explanation.definitionFit: A tomcat uses a tray of absorbent granules as its indoor toilet.

clue.text: Copper sitting on throw is comfortable

indicators.note: in a down clue a piece sitting on another is placed above it

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
to shy is to toss or fling

explanation.surface: A policeman perched on a blanket is nice and cosy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' suggests a policeman and 'throw' a blanket; they are CU and the verb to shy, as at a coconut shy.
explanation.definitionFit: A cushy job or life is easy and undemanding, so pleasantly comfortable.

clue.text: Weasel inside that is foaming at the mouth

indicators.note: something placed inside sits within the walls of another piece, so one is wrapped by the other

parts.note: the abbreviation of the Latin id est
a weasel or a rat is a sneaky, untrustworthy person, an informer

explanation.surface: A rabid weasel indoors, drooling at the jaws.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inside' looks like 'indoors' but places RAT within i.e., the everyday abbreviation of Latin id est, 'that is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone foaming at the mouth is figuratively in a rage, furious enough to splutter, which is what irate means.

clue.text: Fat bear is regularly wanting supplies of food

parts.note: lard is pig fat

indicators.note: taking letters at regular intervals means every other one

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A plump bear is always after something to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fat' reads as describing the bear but is the noun LARD.
explanation.definitionFit: A larder is a pantry for storing food, and by extension the stock of provisions kept there.

clue.text: This writer is against a certain course of action

indicators.note: against can mean right up next to, so one piece stands beside another

parts.note: the setter refers to themself as this writer, so ME
taken as written
sure means certain

explanation.surface: The author declares opposition to a particular plan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Against' looks like opposition but means beside; 'a certain course of action' tempts you to read 'certain' as part of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A measure is a step or plan taken to achieve an end, such as a government measure.

clue.text: Law they broke getting rich

indicators.note: something broke has been smashed, so these letters are scattered and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Criminals broke the law and made a fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broke' also suggests penniless, a neat contrast with the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Wealthy people have plenty of money and possessions, so they are rich.

clue.text: Moving screen — unknown actors stand in front of this

definitions.text: actors stand in front of this

indicators.note: things that are moving shift position, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
algebra's unknowns are x, y and z

explanation.surface: A film on a screen where unknown actors pose in front of the camera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moving screen' suggests cinema, but 'Moving' is the anagram signal and 'unknown' adds Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Stage sets and painted backdrops form the backdrop that performers play before in a theatre.
